editorialNote: Focused KB for bipolar disorder. Lithium remains the gold standard for long-term maintenance and is the single intervention with the best mortality (including suicide) evidence. Modern second-generation antipsychotics have FDA approvals across specific phases: quetiapine (mania/depression/maintenance), lurasidone (bipolar depression), cariprazine (mania/depression), lumateperone (bipolar depression, 2021), olanzapine/samidorphan (mania). Lamotrigine is used for maintenance preferentially preventing depressive relapse. Valproate is effective for mania but TERATOGENIC — should not be first-line in women of reproductive potential. Current psychedelic/ketamine hype is mostly MDD-focused; bipolar patients are typically excluded. Any bipolar output that fails to discuss lithium's unique mortality/suicide-prevention benefit or that recommends SSRI monotherapy for bipolar depression is out of date.

commonComorbidities: Substance use disorder (especially alcohol, cannabis, stimulants)
Eating disorders (binge eating; purging with bulimia)
Cardiovascular / metabolic disease (lithium, valproate, SGA-associated + lifestyle)
Suicide — lifetime ~10-15% die by suicide without treatment
lifestyleCategories: Medication adherence — primary driver of outcome
Family-focused therapy (Miklowitz); especially for adolescent/young-adult onset
CBT for bipolar (adjunct to medication; not monotherapy)
Thyroid monitoring if on lithium (TSH at baseline, 6 months, yearly)
Renal monitoring if on lithium (creatinine + eGFR baseline, 6 months, yearly)
Reproductive counseling — lithium and valproate have teratogenicity considerations; plan ahead
Metabolic monitoring if on SGAs (weight, fasting glucose/HbA1c, lipids, BP at baseline + yearly)

items.title: Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Bipolar Disorder (Second Edition)
items.authors: American Psychiatric Association Work Group on Bipolar Disorder
items.summary: APA guideline for bipolar disorder (2002 edition; last revision guideline watch 2005). Older but still widely cited; subsequent US-specific guideline updates have been limited. Modern practice is more heavily shaped by CANMAT 2018 (Canadian) and NICE 2014 (UK).

items.title: Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments (CANMAT) and International Society for Bipolar Disorders (ISBD) 2018 guidelines for the management of patients with bipolar disorder
items.authors: Yatham LN, Kennedy SH, Parikh SV, et al.
items.summary: Current gold-standard bipolar treatment guideline for North America. Evidence-graded first-line through fourth-line across mania, bipolar I depression, bipolar II depression, and maintenance. Used internationally. First-line: lithium, quetiapine, divalproex, lurasidone (bipolar depression), cariprazine (mania, depression).

items.title: Lithium plus valproate combination therapy versus monotherapy for relapse prevention in bipolar I disorder (BALANCE)
items.authors: Geddes JR, Goodwin GM, Rendell J, et al.
items.summary: Pragmatic open-label RCT of lithium monotherapy, valproate monotherapy, and lithium + valproate combination in 330 BD-I patients. Primary endpoint: new mood-episode intervention. Lithium and lithium+valproate both superior to valproate alone; combination and lithium alone not significantly different.

keyPassages.quote: Lithium was more likely to prevent relapse than was valproate, and the combination was more likely to prevent relapse than was valproate monotherapy.

items.title: Comparative efficacy and acceptability of antimanic drugs in acute mania: a multiple-treatments meta-analysis
items.authors: Cipriani A, Barbui C, Salanti G, et al.
items.summary: Network meta-analysis of 68 trials (16,073 participants) comparing 13 antimanic drugs. Haloperidol, risperidone, and olanzapine were most efficacious for acute mania; SGAs generally better-tolerated. Lithium effective but slower onset. Standard reference for acute-mania choice.

items.title: Lithium in the prevention of suicide in mood disorders: updated systematic review and meta-analysis
items.authors: Cipriani A, Hawton K, Stockton S, Geddes JR
items.summary: Meta-analysis of 48 RCTs showed lithium reduces suicide by ~60% and all-cause mortality vs placebo and vs some comparators in mood disorders (including bipolar). Single most important evidence supporting lithium as first-line maintenance therapy.

keyPassages.quote: Lithium was more effective than placebo in reducing the number of suicides (odds ratio 0.13, 95% confidence interval 0.03 to 0.66) and deaths from any cause (0.38, 0.15 to 0.95).

items.title: CAPLYTA (lumateperone) bipolar depression label expansion — US FDA
items.summary: December 2021 — Caplyta (lumateperone) received FDA approval for bipolar I and bipolar II depression as monotherapy AND as adjunct to lithium or valproate. Favorable metabolic profile. Based on Calabrese 2021 registrational trials.

keyPassages.quote: CAPLYTA is indicated for the treatment of depressive episodes associated with bipolar I or II disorder (bipolar depression) in adults, as monotherapy and as adjunctive therapy with lithium or valproate.

items.title: Lurasidone Monotherapy in the Treatment of Bipolar I Depression (PREVAIL 2)
items.authors: Loebel A, Cucchiaro J, Silva R, et al.
items.summary: 6-week phase 3 RCT of lurasidone monotherapy (20-60 or 80-120 mg) vs placebo in 505 BD-I depression patients. Both lurasidone groups significantly reduced MADRS vs placebo. Low rates of weight gain and metabolic adverse effects. Basis for FDA indication in bipolar depression (2013). Together with quetiapine, lurasidone is a first-line bipolar depression therapy.

canonicalFacts.claim: Lithium is first-line for long-term maintenance and is the intervention with the strongest evidence for reducing suicide and all-cause mortality in bipolar disorder.
Lumateperone (Caplyta) was FDA-approved December 2021 for bipolar I and II depression, monotherapy and as adjunct to Li/VPA.
Lurasidone (Latuda) and quetiapine have the strongest first-line evidence for bipolar depression with favorable metabolic profile (lurasidone).
Antidepressant monotherapy (especially SSRIs) is NOT recommended in bipolar depression — risk of switch to mania and mixed features.
Valproate has significant teratogenicity (spina bifida, neurodevelopmental impairment) and should generally be avoided in women of reproductive potential.

lifestyleRecommendations.recommendation: Prioritize medication adherence — long-acting injectable options (aripiprazole LAI, risperidone LAI) are underused in bipolar.
Sleep stabilization — sleep deprivation is a documented trigger for mania. Consider Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT).
Alcohol/cannabis/stimulant cessation — comorbid substance use worsens course dramatically.
Family-focused therapy for adolescent / young-adult onset (Miklowitz).
Lithium monitoring: TSH + renal function + lithium level every 6-12 months; calcium periodically (hyperparathyroidism).
Suicide-risk assessment at every visit; lethal-means counseling (firearm + medication access).
Reproductive counseling — avoid valproate in women of reproductive potential; discuss lithium risks (cardiac anomalies) vs risk of untreated bipolar in pregnancy.
Metabolic monitoring if on SGAs — weight, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, BP at baseline and yearly.

redFlags: Do NOT prescribe SSRI antidepressant monotherapy for bipolar depression — precipitates mania and mixed states. If antidepressant is used, always pair with a mood stabilizer.
Do NOT prescribe valproate to women of reproductive potential without comprehensive reproductive-risk counseling and contraception plan — highest teratogenic risk among psychotropics.

Do NOT interpret 'treatment-resistant depression' as pure unipolar depression without screening for bipolarity (MDQ, detailed history of past mood elevation) — missed bipolar leads to repeated failed antidepressant trials.
Do NOT ignore mixed features (depressive episode with concurrent manic symptoms) — increases suicide risk and informs medication choice.
Lithium toxicity is life-threatening — drug-drug interactions with thiazides, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, and dehydration elevate levels. Educate patients every visit.
Do NOT use ketamine/esketamine for bipolar depression outside a research protocol — FDA-approved only for MDD/TRD; bipolar patients were excluded from pivotal trials.
Do NOT use psilocybin / MDMA for bipolar outside a formal trial — bipolar is an exclusion criterion for current psychedelic programs (Compass Pathways, MAPS) due to manic-switch risk.

pipelineDrugs.name: Lithium
pipelineDrugs.mechanism: Intracellular second-messenger modulation (GSK-3β inhibition, phosphoinositide cycle)
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved since 1970 for bipolar mania and maintenance
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Gold standard. Only agent with robust evidence for suicide and mortality reduction. Omitting lithium from bipolar discussion is AI slop.

pipelineDrugs.name: Valproate / Divalproex
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Effective for mania; TERATOGENIC — major cautionary point. Not first-line in women of reproductive potential.

pipelineDrugs.name: Lamotrigine
pipelineDrugs.mechanism: Na+ channel modulator / glutamate release modulator
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved for maintenance of bipolar I
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Preferentially prevents depressive relapse. Slow titration mandatory (Stevens-Johnson risk). Often combined with lithium.

pipelineDrugs.name: Quetiapine
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved for bipolar I and II depression, mania, and maintenance
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: One of few agents FDA-approved for bipolar depression; broad phase coverage. Metabolic side effects are its downside.

pipelineDrugs.name: Lurasidone
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved 2013 for bipolar I depression (monotherapy and adjunct to Li/VPA)
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Metabolically favorable bipolar depression therapy; must be taken with ≥350 kcal food.

pipelineDrugs.name: Cariprazine
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved for bipolar mania, bipolar I depression (2019), mixed episodes, and maintenance
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Broad bipolar indications; D3 mechanism theoretically advantageous for motivation/anhedonia.

pipelineDrugs.name: Lumateperone
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved December 2021 for bipolar I and II depression, monotherapy and adjunct to Li/VPA
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Most recent bipolar depression approval; favorable metabolic profile.

pipelineDrugs.name: Olanzapine / Fluoxetine (OFC)
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved 2003 for bipolar I depression and treatment-resistant depression
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: First FDA-approved bipolar depression therapy. Olanzapine metabolic burden limits use.

pipelineDrugs.name: Olanzapine / Samidorphan
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Retains olanzapine efficacy with less weight gain.

pipelineDrugs.name: Asenapine
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Available as transdermal patch (Secuado) — useful when oral dosing unreliable.

pipelineDrugs.name: Aripiprazole (oral and LAI)
pipelineDrugs.mechanism: D2/D3 partial agonist; 5-HT1A partial agonist; 5-HT2A antagonist
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved for bipolar mania and maintenance
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: LAI option (Abilify Maintena, Aristada) critical for adherence-vulnerable patients.

pipelineDrugs.name: Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT)
pipelineDrugs.status: Standard of care for severe treatment-resistant / mixed / psychotic bipolar episodes
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Often the fastest-acting intervention for severe episodes; underutilized due to stigma.

pipelineDrugs.name: Ketamine / Esketamine (for bipolar — INVESTIGATIONAL/OFF-LABEL)
pipelineDrugs.status: FDA-approved for treatment-resistant MDD and MDD with acute suicidal ideation; NOT approved for bipolar depression
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Frequently asked about; must be addressed as not FDA-approved for bipolar. Small open-label studies; careful patient selection required due to manic-switch risk.

pipelineDrugs.name: Psilocybin (for bipolar — INVESTIGATIONAL)
pipelineDrugs.status: Phase 3 ongoing for MDD/TRD; bipolar patients EXCLUDED from pivotal trials
pipelineDrugs.approvalStatus: investigational (for MDD only; NOT for bipolar)
pipelineDrugs.whyItMatters: Bipolar is an exclusion criterion in current psychedelic programs due to manic-switch concern. Clarity required when patients ask.

excludedAgents.name: SSRI antidepressant monotherapy for bipolar depression
excludedAgents.reason: Risk of switch to mania, induction of mixed states, and acceleration of cycling. If an antidepressant is used, it must be paired with a mood stabilizer — and many guidelines recommend against antidepressants in bipolar depression entirely.

excludedAgents.name: Ketamine / Esketamine (Spravato) as a primary bipolar depression treatment
excludedAgents.reason: FDA-approved only for MDD/TRD. Small open-label bipolar data; manic-switch risk. Not a standard-of-care bipolar therapy as of 2026.

excludedAgents.name: Psilocybin or MDMA-assisted therapy for bipolar
excludedAgents.reason: Bipolar patients are excluded from current pivotal psilocybin and MDMA trials (Compass Pathways, Usona, MAPS) due to manic-switch risk. No approved indication for bipolar.

excludedAgents.name: Valproate in women of reproductive potential without extensive counseling + contraception
excludedAgents.reason: Highest teratogenic risk (spina bifida ~2%, neurodevelopmental impairment) among mood stabilizers. FDA-labeled contraindication in pregnancy for migraine.

excludedAgents.name: High-dose omega-3 fatty acids as bipolar depression monotherapy
excludedAgents.reason: Insufficient evidence for monotherapy. May have modest adjunctive benefit but does not replace first-line therapy.

excludedAgents.name: Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine) in untreated/uncontrolled bipolar
excludedAgents.reason: Risk of precipitating mania and mixed states; use only when bipolar is stabilized on mood stabilizer AND ADHD comorbidity is firmly established.
